course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Consequences of Industrialization
unit.description: Study why industrial states built empires, how colonized peoples resisted, how economies were reshaped, and why millions of people migrated.

firstTopic.title: Rationales for Imperialism from 1750 to 1900

topic.title: Economic Imperialism from 1750 to 1900

questions.distinguisher: They describe cheap goods as the “heavy artillery,” a metaphor rather than literal conquest.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, German political philosophers, Manifesto of the Communist Party, 1848
stimulusBlocks.citation: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, Manifesto of the Communist Party, English edition of 1888, trans. Samuel Moore, section I. Project Gutenberg eBook #61.
stimulusBlocks.note: The bourgeoisie are the owners of capital. Marx and Engels use words such as “barbarian” sarcastically, echoing how European capitalists described other peoples. “Chinese walls” refers to China's limits on foreign trade.
stimulusBlocks.text: The bourgeoisie, by the rapid improvement of all instruments of production, by the immensely facilitated means of communication, draws all, even the most barbarian, nations into civilisation. The cheap prices of its commodities are the heavy artillery with which it batters down all Chinese walls, with which it forces the barbarians' intensely obstinate hatred of foreigners to capitulate. It compels all nations, on pain of extinction, to adopt the bourgeois mode of production . . . . In one word, it creates a world after its own image.

choiceExplanations: The phrase is a metaphor for trade barriers.

Western powers sought to open China.
In the 1840s, Britain forced China to open ports after the First Opium War.
questions.distinguisher: Western powers wanted China open, not closed.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 6.5 key concept: economic imperialism, as in the Opium Wars, forced states such as China to open to foreign trade
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Opium Wars, 1839–1860
stimulusBlocks.text:
British merchants sold opium grown in India to China, reversing the flow of silver that had long gone into China. When the Qing official Lin Zexu destroyed British opium stocks in 1839, Britain went to war. British steamships and modern guns defeated Qing forces.

The Treaty of Nanjing in 1842 forced China to give Hong Kong to Britain, open five ports to foreign trade, and pay a large indemnity. A second war from 1856 to 1860 opened more ports and legalized the opium trade. Historians call these unequal treaties because China gained nothing in return.

questions.explanation: The passage says China gained nothing in return.
choiceExplanations: Britain gained Hong Kong.
Only China opened ports.
Britain forced them on China.
The passage says China gained nothing in return.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, economic imperialism in Latin America meant that foreign powers
choices: gained new colonies through a war with Spain

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 6.5 key concept: economic imperialism also took the form of foreign investment, as with British and US investment in Latin America
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing foreign investment in Latin America, 1870–1914
stimulusBlocks.text:
Latin American countries were politically independent by 1900, but much of their economic infrastructure was owned by foreigners. British investors financed railroads, ports, and mines in Argentina, Chile, and Mexico. American companies built banana plantations in Central America and gained great influence over local governments.

Historians describe this as economic imperialism: foreign powers gained profits and influence without formal colonial rule.

In both, foreign powers held economic privileges without full colonial rule.
questions.distinguisher: India was ruled directly, unlike Latin America.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why did British merchants sell opium in China?
choices: To reverse the outflow of silver paid for Chinese goods
To weaken the Qing army before a planned invasion of China
Because the Qing government had asked them to supply it
To raise money for schools run by Christian missionaries
questions.explanation: British merchants wanted to stop paying for tea, silk, and porcelain with silver.
choiceExplanations: British merchants wanted to stop paying for tea, silk, and porcelain with silver.
The passage does not link opium sales to an invasion plan.
The Qing banned opium, and Lin Zexu destroyed it.
The passage does not mention missionary schools.
questions.distinguisher: Opium did harm Chinese society, but the passage presents the merchants' motive as economic.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 6.5 key concept: Britain used military force to open China to trade in opium and other goods
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Opium Wars, 1839–1860
stimulusBlocks.text:
In the early 1800s, British merchants paid for Chinese tea, silk, and porcelain largely with silver. To reverse the flow, they sold opium grown in British India to Chinese buyers. As addiction spread and silver left China, the Qing official Lin Zexu destroyed more than 20,000 chests of opium at Guangzhou in 1839. Britain sent warships, and the Qing were defeated in the First Opium War.

The Treaty of Nanjing in 1842 forced China to pay an indemnity, give Hong Kong to Britain, and open five ports to foreign trade. A second war, ending in 1860, opened more ports and allowed foreign merchants and missionaries to travel inland.

questions.prompt: Which result of the wars best shows the weakening of Qing control over China's trade?
choices: The Qing agreed to pay a yearly tax to British merchants
The Qing opened an embassy in London to negotiate
The Qing abolished the civil service examination system
The Qing had to open ports and give up Hong Kong
questions.explanation: Opening treaty ports and ceding Hong Kong placed parts of China's trade and territory under foreign terms.
choiceExplanations: The Qing paid an indemnity after losing, but a payment is not a loss of control over ports.
An embassy was a diplomatic step, not a sign of lost control.
The examination system lasted until 1905.
Opening treaty ports and ceding Hong Kong placed parts of China's trade and territory under foreign terms.
questions.distinguisher: The Qing did pay an indemnity, but opening ports and ceding territory more directly limited their control.
